Is the implant the visible tooth?
sections.heading: What is a dental implant?

visibleCopy.standard:
A dental implant is a manufactured fixture placed in the jaw to support a replacement tooth or teeth. It can support a crown, a bridge or some types of removable denture.

The implant is not the whole replacement tooth. A connector called an abutment may sit between the fixture and the visible restoration. The exact design varies, and only an assessment can establish whether implant treatment is an appropriate option for a particular person.
visibleCopy.short: A dental implant is a fixture placed in the jaw to support a crown, bridge or some types of denture.

sections.job: Explain the fixture, abutment and restoration while distinguishing manufactured components from living anatomy.
ownedQuestions: What are the parts of an implant restoration?
Which parts are biological and which are manufactured?
sections.heading: Three roles, working as one restoration.

visibleCopy.standard:
A generic implant restoration can be understood in three layers. The fixture sits within the jaw. The abutment connects the fixture to the replacement tooth. The restoration is the part used to replace the missing tooth or teeth.

Bone, gum, neighbouring teeth, nerves and sinus spaces are living biological structures. Their shape and health vary from person to person. This explanation shows relationships only; it does not represent your anatomy or propose an implant position.
visibleCopy.transcript: Natural-tooth context: a tooth has a crown visible above the gum and roots within the jaw. Missing-tooth context: the space and surrounding biological structures are shown without measurements. Fixture: a manufactured component positioned within a generic jaw illustration. Abutment: the connector above the fixture. Restoration: a crown is shown as one possible visible replacement; bridges and implant-retained dentures use different configurations.

sections.heading: Suitability cannot be read from a checklist.

visibleCopy.standard:
An implant assessment looks at the whole clinical situation, not a single yes-or-no factor. A clinician may consider the health of the teeth and gums, the available space and anatomy, the bite, medical history and medicines, smoking, healing and disease risks, the ability to clean and maintain the result, and what the person hopes treatment will achieve.

These factors interact. A public page, questionnaire, photograph, scan upload or 3D model cannot decide whether implants are suitable for you.

General health, medical history and medicines
Smoking and other modifiable risk factors

sections.job: Explain the purpose of examination, records and indication-based imaging without promising a local technology workflow.
ownedQuestions: How are dental implants planned?
Does every implant patient need a CBCT scan?
sections.heading: Use each record to answer a clinical question.

visibleCopy.standard:
Planning begins with a conversation, medical and dental history, and a clinical examination. Photographs, models, digital scans or radiographs may be recommended when they add information needed for the decision.

CBCT is a three-dimensional X-ray examination. It should be prescribed for an individual clinical reason rather than treated as an automatic website promise. Where imaging is justified, it helps the clinician assess relevant anatomy and plan care; the scan still requires professional interpretation and does not make the decision by itself.

The result of planning should be an explanation of realistic options, important risks and limitations, likely stages and costs before treatment is agreed.

sections.heading: There is more than one way to manage a missing tooth.

visibleCopy.standard: Implants, bridges, dentures and sometimes accepting or monitoring a space solve different problems. The most appropriate options depend on oral health, anatomy, function, appearance, maintenance, cost and what matters to the person. This comparison is a starting point, not a recommendation.

sections.job: Present potential benefits, limitations and material risks in balanced language without replacing consent.
ownedQuestions: What are the possible benefits and risks of dental implants?
Can implants fail?
sections.heading: Benefits matter. So do limitations and risks.

visibleCopy.standard:
An implant-supported restoration may provide a fixed replacement, or improve support for some removable dentures. Some designs avoid relying on neighbouring teeth for support. Those potential benefits have to be weighed against surgery, healing, maintenance, cost and the possibility of biological or mechanical complications.

Risks can include failure of the implant to integrate with bone, infection or inflammation around the implant, changes in gum or bone, injury to nearby structures, and loosening, wear or fracture of components. Additional procedures or later repair, replacement or removal may be needed. The risks differ between people and plans, and this summary is not a substitute for individual consent.

sections.job: Explain long-term cleaning, monitoring and repair pathways without prescribing a personal schedule or managing complications remotely.
ownedQuestions: How are dental implants cared for?
Do implants need professional maintenance?
sections.heading: Implants are maintained, not forgotten.

visibleCopy.standard:
Implant-supported teeth and the tissues around them need daily cleaning and professional monitoring. Reviews may assess cleaning access, gum health, the stability of the restoration and changes that need attention. The frequency and methods should be tailored to the person, the restoration and their risk factors.

Implants do not remove the possibility of gum inflammation, bone loss, wear or component problems. If an implant, surrounding gum or restoration feels different, becomes painful, swollen, loose or difficult to clean, contact the treating dental team rather than relying on generic online advice.

carePrinciples: Clean the implant-supported restoration and gumline using the method shown by the dental team
Attend risk-based professional monitoring and maintenance
Manage modifiable risks such as smoking and active gum disease with professional support
Report pain, swelling, bleeding, looseness or a change in the restoration promptly

faqs.question: Am I suitable for dental implants?
faqs.answer: That cannot be decided from a website, questionnaire, photograph or generic 3D model. A clinician needs to assess oral health, relevant anatomy, medical history, maintenance and the available alternatives.

faqs.question: Does every Implant patient need a CBCT scan?
faqs.answer: No imaging examination should be automatic. A clinician decides which records are justified after taking a history and examining you; any CBCT image also requires professional interpretation.

faqs.question: How long does Implant treatment take?
faqs.answer: There is no reliable universal timeline. The sequence depends on the starting condition, the replacement being planned, healing and whether any preparatory treatment is needed. A personal estimate follows assessment.

faqs.question: How long do dental implants last?
faqs.answer: No lifespan can be promised. Long-term function depends on biological health, cleaning, risk factors, maintenance and the condition of the restoration and components; repair or replacement may be needed.

faqs.question: What are the alternatives to dental implants?
faqs.answer: Depending on the clinical situation, alternatives may include a dental bridge, a removable denture, or accepting and monitoring the space. The trade-offs require assessment rather than a universal ranking.

newWeosBackTeach.champagneEvidence: The Implant-vs-bridge-vs-denture comparison contains multiple independently risky cells even though it looks like one component.
newWeosBackTeach.tenantNeutralRule: Every cell in a treatment comparison is an atomic claim with its own owner, source, reviewer state and hash.
newWeosBackTeach.why: A visually balanced table can still drift into an unsupported recommendation if one cell changes independently.
newWeosBackTeach.captainInput: Which treatment options actually exist and who can approve clinical trade-offs.
newWeosBackTeach.routerGovernance: Block publication when any rendered comparison cell lacks current approval or hash parity.

newWeosBackTeach.champagneEvidence: Interactive 3D and case proof are unavailable, but only 3D has a complete static semantic replacement; proof must disappear entirely.
newWeosBackTeach.tenantNeutralRule: Capability-off behavior is job-specific: substitute an equivalent accessible explanation only when it preserves the same truth; otherwise fail closed with no shell.
newWeosBackTeach.why: Automatic placeholders can fabricate capability, proof or meaning even when no false sentence is written.
newWeosBackTeach.captainInput: Which capabilities and genuine assets are available for the tenant.
newWeosBackTeach.routerGovernance: Require an explicit off-state contract for every optional semantic section before composition.

newWeosBackTeach.champagneEvidence: The Implant overview has many live child routes that can easily repeat consultation, full-arch, grafting, sedation and aftercare detail.
newWeosBackTeach.tenantNeutralRule: A parent treatment page owns the balanced overview and a fixed question budget; child routes own depth and must not be cannibalised by generated parent copy.
newWeosBackTeach.why: A route graph alone does not stop autonomous copy from answering the same query in full on every related page.
newWeosBackTeach.captainInput: Which subservices are real and which pages deserve independent ownership.
newWeosBackTeach.routerGovernance: Compile question ownership before generation and reject cross-route answer-depth collisions.
